title: OTLP logs export: own OTLP/HTTP JSON exporter on the Go standard library (replaces the @opentelemetry/* family)
An own OTLP/HTTP JSON logs exporter; the OpenTelemetry SDK is not linked
Records are explicit; the diagnostic log is never exported; no ambient OTEL_* configuration
Nothing leaves the machine by default: each flow is a visible opt-in setting, one off-switch covers all, and feedback shows what will be sent (owner decision, 2026-11-18)
A batch is OTLP logs JSON with the expected fields and headers, and no attribute the caller did not supply
The service alone and a disabled consumer open no connection, start no goroutine and read no identity
Two channels never share a request, a header or a record
OTEL_* environment variables change nothing and redirects are not followed
Emit never waits for the network and a full queue drops and counts
Requests stay under the byte ceiling, run one at a time in order, and an oversized record is rejected whole
Transient statuses are retried inside the deadline, other statuses are not, and the deadline ends a hung request
Shutdown returns at its deadline, cancels the request, reports the loss and leaves no goroutine
Diagnostics never contain record content, attribute values or header values
Invalid channel options fail the creating component only, with a field-named error
Telemetry requests use the HTTP client the harness supplies, so the proxy policy applies
The JSON fixtures decode with the official OTLP message types in a separate test-only module
Withdrawn consent closes a channel without sending: the request in flight is cancelled, the queue is discarded and counted, and no connection follows

reason: Upstream imports it only for the Attributes type and never creates a tracer, meter or global provider; the Go channel takes attributes as slog.Attr values, so no OpenTelemetry API package is needed.
It supplies the severity enum and the logger type for log records; the Go record carries a slog.Level that the own exporter maps to OTLP severity numbers 5, 9, 13 and 17.
Its only use is ExportResultCode, which tells a successful export callback from a failed one; in Go the send returns an error value, so the package has no counterpart.

It provides the HTTP exporter shell, the Node HTTP agent and timeout and compression defaults read partly from OTEL_* variables; the own exporter posts through net/http with a harness-supplied client and reads nothing from the environment.

It encodes log records as OTLP JSON and is also called once per record just to measure size; the own exporter encodes each record once with encoding/json and keeps the bytes, which gives exact byte-bounded batching.

Its one function attaches service name, version and the anonymous user id to a channel; the Go channel takes a resource function that is evaluated at the first accepted record, so identity is not read before something is sent.

It provides the logger provider and count-only batch processor that upstream had to wrap with its own byte-bounded processor; one Go channel type with a bounded queue and count-and-byte batching replaces both.

title: Seven OpenTelemetry packages pinned to exact versions of one coordinated release, four from the experimental 0.x tree; one consumer declares sdk-logs without importing it

reason: The Go design links no OpenTelemetry SDK, so there is no coordinated release train or experimental API to follow; the exporter is harness code on the standard library.

title: Two HTTP transports for one protocol: the SDK transport cannot be cancelled, so ordinary events use a second transport on got that re-implements retry, gzip and the response limit

reason: The own exporter has one transport on net/http, where the request context cancels both the request in flight and the retry wait, so a second cancellable transport is not needed.

title: Byte-bounded batching is re-implemented around a count-only SDK: each record is encoded twice, sizes are over-counted, and the watchdog cannot free a stuck request slot

reason: The exporter owns the encoder, so each record is encoded once and counted exactly, every channel is bounded by count and bytes, and the per-request deadline cancels the request instead of only warning.

title: Unused SDK machinery is neutralised by hand: metrics and trace SDKs come in transitively, a self-observability meter is passed as undefined, and OTEL_* variables still set compression and timeout

reason: The Go exporter implements the logs signal only and reads no setting from the environment, so there is no unused meter or tracer to switch off and no ambient variable that can change where or how data is sent.
